title: Merge Sort
body:
Divide and conquer, and the reliable one. Split the [[Array]] in half, sort each half by
calling yourself, then **merge** the two sorted halves into one. $O(n \log n)$ in the best,
average, *and* worst case, with no bad input that can trip it. The price is $O(n)$ extra
space for the merge.

```
        [38, 27, 43, 3, 9, 82, 10]
       /                          \
  [38, 27, 43]                [3, 9, 82, 10]
     split                        split
  [38] [27, 43]              [3, 9]  [82, 10]
       ...                        ...
  merge back up:
  [27, 38, 43]                [3, 9, 10, 82]
       \                          /
        [3, 9, 10, 27, 38, 43, 82]
```

## The merge

The interesting half is not the splitting, it is the merging, and it only works because both
inputs are already sorted. Walk a finger along each half and repeatedly take the smaller of
the two front elements.

```java
void merge(int[] a, int lo, int mid, int hi, int[] tmp) {
    int i = lo, j = mid + 1, k = lo;
    while (i <= mid && j <= hi)
        tmp[k++] = (a[i] <= a[j]) ? a[i++] : a[j++];
    while (i <= mid) tmp[k++] = a[i++];      // leftovers from the left half
    while (j <= hi)  tmp[k++] = a[j++];      // or from the right
    for (k = lo; k <= hi; k++) a[k] = tmp[k];
}

void mergeSort(int[] a, int lo, int hi, int[] tmp) {
    if (lo >= hi) return;                     // one element is already sorted
    int mid = (lo + hi) / 2;
    mergeSort(a, lo, mid, tmp);
    mergeSort(a, mid + 1, hi, tmp);
    merge(a, lo, mid, hi, tmp);
}
```

Each merge touches every element in the range once, so a merge is $O(n)$. Note `<=` rather
than `<` in the comparison: taking from the left half on ties is what makes the sort stable.

## Why $O(n \log n)$

The [[Recursion]] halves the range every level, so there are $\log_2 n$ levels. Every level
merges a total of $n$ elements, whichever way the ranges are carved up. $n$ work per level,
$\log n$ levels, so $n \log n$ overall, and nothing about the input can change that: the
splitting is positional, not value-dependent. Compare [[Quick Sort]], where the partition
*is* value-dependent and a bad pivot ruins the level count.

## Trade-offs

| | |
|---|---|
| Time | $O(n \log n)$ best, average, and worst |
| Space | $O(n)$ extra for the scratch array |
| Stable | yes, equal elements keep their original order |
| In place | no |

The $O(n)$ space is the real objection, and it is why [[Quick Sort]] is usually the default
for arrays in memory. Merge sort wins whenever the guarantee matters more than the memory,
and it wins outright on [[Linked List]]s, where merging is pointer relinking and needs no
extra array at all. It is also the basis of external sorting: when the data does not fit in
memory, you sort chunks that do and merge the sorted runs off disk.
